title: How to Write a Brand Voice Sheet That Keeps AI Drafts Usable
excerpt: Most AI drafts get rewritten because the brief was empty. This guide covers the sections a brand voice sheet needs, how to feed it into every prompt, and how to keep it current from a rejection log.
body: Teams blame the model when drafts come back generic, but the usual cause is an empty brief. A prompt that says write a product description returns the average of everything the model has read, which is the tone nobody wants. The fix is not a cleverer prompt. It is a one page voice sheet that travels with every request: who you are writing for, what you never claim, and what a good paragraph from your own catalog looks like. With that sheet in the prompt, first drafts need edits rather than rewrites.

Six sections are enough. Audience: one paragraph on who buys and what problem they are solving today, written as a situation instead of a demographic. Banned language: the words and claims you refuse, including superlatives and absolute claims about durability, health or delivery dates. Sentence shape: a target length range and a rule about openings, because rhythm is what readers read as a brand. Product naming: how you refer to the item, the material and the size, so a draft never calls one product by three names. Numbers: imperial, metric or both, and how you round. Example: one real paragraph from your site, marked as the standard.

Put the sheet in the prompt every time, not in a style guide that lives in a folder nobody opens. Prefix each request with the audience and banned language sections, paste the example paragraph, and ask for the same shape. When a draft comes back, score it against the sheet before judging the writing: audience addressed, no banned claims, naming consistent, numbers formatted, length inside the range. Scoring separates two problems. A draft that fails the sheet needs another pass, while a draft that passes and still reads badly is a taste problem, and taste needs a human.

Keep a rejection log. Each time you discard a draft, write one line naming which section of the sheet failed to prevent it. After twenty entries the pattern is clear: usually claims language or naming, rarely tone. Every repeated failure is a missing rule, so add it to the sheet instead of repeating the correction in review comments. The sheet should grow for the first month and then stabilise. If it keeps growing, the real gap is that nobody agreed on who the audience is.

Set the boundary on where generation stops. Specification tables, pricing, materials and anything regulated should be copied from source data, never produced by a model. A voice sheet makes prose consistent; it does not make facts reliable, and the cheapest failure is a confident wrong number on a live page. Track two numbers: the share of drafts published without a full rewrite, and average editing minutes per draft. If editing time has not dropped after a month, the sheet is not reaching the prompt, which is a process fix.

Give the sheet an owner and a review date. Voice drifts when a new product line, a new market or a new hire arrives, and a sheet nobody maintains becomes a document people ignore. Quarterly is enough for most stores: read the last ten pieces against the sheet and adjust one rule.
